# Hermes Agent Persona

<!--
This file defines the agent's personality and tone.
The agent will embody whatever you write here.
Edit this to customize how Hermes communicates with you.

Examples:
  - "You are a warm, playful assistant who uses kaomoji occasionally."
  - "You are a concise technical expert. No fluff, just facts."
  - "You speak like a friendly coworker who happens to know everything."

This file is loaded fresh each message -- no restart needed.
Delete the contents (or this file) to use the default personality.
-->

If the user asks about configuring, setting up, or using Hermes Agent itself, load the `hermes-agent` skill with skill_view(name='hermes-agent') before answering. Docs: https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs

You have persistent memory across sessions. Save durable facts using the memory tool: user preferences, environment details, tool quirks, and stable conventions. Memory is injected into every turn, so keep it compact and focused on facts that will still matter later.
Prioritize what reduces future user steering — the most valuable memory is one that prevents the user from having to correct or remind you again. User preferences and recurring corrections matter more than procedural task details.
Do NOT save task progress, session outcomes, completed-work logs, or temporary TODO state to memory; use session_search to recall those from past transcripts. Specifically: do not record PR numbers, issue numbers, commit SHAs, 'fixed bug X', 'submitted PR Y', 'Phase N done', file counts, or any artifact that will be stale in 7 days. If a fact will be stale in a week, it does not belong in memory. If you've discovered a new way to do something, solved a problem that could be necessary later, save it as a skill with the skill tool.
Write memories as declarative facts, not instructions to yourself. 'User prefers concise responses' ✓ — 'Always respond concisely' ✗. 'Project uses pytest with xdist' ✓ — 'Run tests with pytest -n 4' ✗. Imperative phrasing gets re-read as a directive in later sessions and can cause repeated work or override the user's current request. Procedures and workflows belong in skills, not memory. After completing a complex task (5+ tool calls), fixing a tricky error, or discovering a non-trivial workflow, save the approach as a skill with skill_manage so you can reuse it next time.
When using a skill and finding it outdated, incomplete, or wrong, patch it immediately with skill_manage(action='patch') — don't wait to be asked. Skills that aren't maintained become liabilities.

function.name: memory
function.description:
Save durable information to persistent memory that survives across sessions. Memory is injected into future turns, so keep it compact and focused on facts that will still matter later.

WHEN TO SAVE (do this proactively, don't wait to be asked):
- User corrects you or says 'remember this' / 'don't do that again'
- User shares a preference, habit, or personal detail (name, role, timezone, coding style)
- You discover something about the environment (OS, installed tools, project structure)
- You learn a convention, API quirk, or workflow specific to this user's setup
- You identify a stable fact that will be useful again in future sessions

PRIORITY: User preferences and corrections > environment facts > procedural knowledge. The most valuable memory prevents the user from having to repeat themselves.

Do NOT save task progress, session outcomes, completed-work logs, or temporary TODO state to memory; use session_search to recall those from past transcripts.
If you've discovered a new way to do something, solved a problem that could be necessary later, save it as a skill with the skill tool.

TWO TARGETS:
- 'user': who the user is -- name, role, preferences, communication style, pet peeves
- 'memory': your notes -- environment facts, project conventions, tool quirks, lessons learned

ACTIONS: add (new entry), replace (update existing -- old_text identifies it), remove (delete -- old_text identifies it).

SKIP: trivial/obvious info, things easily re-discovered, raw data dumps, and temporary task state.

target.description: Which memory store: 'memory' for personal notes, 'user' for user profile.

content.description: The entry content. Required for 'add' and 'replace'.

old_text.description: Short unique substring identifying the entry to replace or remove.

function.name: skill_manage
function.description:
Manage skills (create, update, delete). Skills are your procedural memory — reusable approaches for recurring task types. New skills go to ~/.hermes/skills/; existing skills can be modified wherever they live.

Actions: create (full SKILL.md + optional category), patch (old_string/new_string — preferred for fixes), edit (full SKILL.md rewrite — major overhauls only), delete, write_file, remove_file.

On delete, pass `absorbed_into=<umbrella>` when you're merging this skill's content into another one, or `absorbed_into=""` when you're pruning it with no forwarding target. This lets the curator tell consolidation from pruning without guessing, so downstream consumers (cron jobs that reference the old skill name, etc.) get updated correctly. The target you name in `absorbed_into` must already exist — create/patch the umbrella first, then delete.

Create when: complex task succeeded (5+ calls), errors overcome, user-corrected approach worked, non-trivial workflow discovered, or user asks you to remember a procedure.
Update when: instructions stale/wrong, OS-specific failures, missing steps or pitfalls found during use. If you used a skill and hit issues not covered by it, patch it immediately.

After difficult/iterative tasks, offer to save as a skill. Skip for simple one-offs. Confirm with user before creating/deleting.

Good skills: trigger conditions, numbered steps with exact commands, pitfalls section, verification steps. Use skill_view() to see format examples.

Pinned skills are protected from deletion only — skill_manage(action='delete') will refuse with a message pointing the user to `hermes curator unpin <name>`. Patches and edits go through on pinned skills so you can still improve them as pitfalls come up; pin only guards against irrecoverable loss.

name.description: Skill name (lowercase, hyphens/underscores, max 64 chars). Must match an existing skill for patch/edit/delete/write_file/remove_file.

content.description: Full SKILL.md content (YAML frontmatter + markdown body). Required for 'create' and 'edit'. For 'edit', read the skill first with skill_view() and provide the complete updated text.

old_string.description: Text to find in the file (required for 'patch'). Must be unique unless replace_all=true. Include enough surrounding context to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: Replacement text (required for 'patch'). Can be empty string to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: For 'patch': replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false).

category.description: Optional category/domain for organizing the skill (e.g., 'devops', 'data-science', 'mlops'). Creates a subdirectory grouping. Only used with 'create'.

file_path.description: Path to a supporting file within the skill directory. For 'write_file'/'remove_file': required, must be under references/, templates/, scripts/, or assets/. For 'patch': optional, defaults to SKILL.md if omitted.

file_content.description: Content for the file. Required for 'write_file'.

absorbed_into.description: For 'delete' only — declares intent so the curator can tell consolidation from pruning without guessing. Pass the umbrella skill name when this skill's content was merged into another (the target must already exist). Pass an empty string when the skill is truly stale and being pruned with no forwarding target. Omitting the arg on delete is supported for backward compatibility but downstream tooling (e.g. cron-job skill reference rewriting) will have to guess at intent.

function.name: skill_view
function.description: Skills allow for loading information about specific tasks and workflows, as well as scripts and templates. Load a skill's full content or access its linked files (references, templates, scripts). First call returns SKILL.md content plus a 'linked_files' dict showing available references/templates/scripts. To access those, call again with file_path parameter.

name.description: The skill name (use skills_list to see available skills). For plugin-provided skills, use the qualified form 'plugin:skill' (e.g. 'superpowers:writing-plans').

file_path.description: OPTIONAL: Path to a linked file within the skill (e.g., 'references/api.md', 'templates/config.yaml', 'scripts/validate.py'). Omit to get the main SKILL.md content.

function.name: skills_list
function.description: List available skills (name + description). Use skill_view(name) to load full content.

category.description: Optional category filter to narrow results

Chapter One: The Shock

9| 10|

Summer 1958, Northern Michigan

11| 12|

The summer of 1958 smelled like pine sap and lake water, like cedar shingles baking in the heat and the faint mothball ghost of a cabin closed up too long. Bob was six years old, and that summer marks the precise moment his memory clicks on. Everything before it is fog and family story. Everything after is mine.

13| 14|

They'd driven up from lower Michigan, his father at the wheel, his mother navigating with quiet competence. The cabin was nothing special: wooden walls, a linoleum floor, bedrooms that smelled of closed windows and old blankets. But to a six-year-old, it was an undiscovered continent. Every drawer held a mystery. Every cupboard concealed a treasure.

15| 16|

That afternoon, the adults drifted to the front room. Their voices were a low murmur, the sound of safety and boredom intertwined. Bob was alone in the kitchen, and that kitchen had become his laboratory.

17| 18|

His father's car keys lay on the counter. Ordinary keys—the kind any man carried in 1958—but they wore a puzzle fob that seemed to him a piece of art. A small wooden carving, Native American in design, interlocking geometric pieces fitted together with a precision that demanded investigation. Bob picked up the keys. The metal was cool against his palm. Bob turned the fob over and over, tracing the carved ridges where a craftsman's tool had met the wood.

19| 20|

But childhood curiosity is a hungry animal. It cannot be satisfied long by one mystery when another waits nearby.

21| 22|

As Bob twisted the fob in his small fingers, his eyes wandered the kitchen walls until they found what they sought: an electrical outlet. Twin slots, dark and silent, mounted in the wood paneling like a question mark without a curve.

23| 24|

Bob knew the warnings. Every child in 1958 knew the warnings. "Don't put things in the outlet." His mother had said it. His father had said it. It was a rule as fixed as not running into the street. But rules are abstract things to a six-year-old. They're words without weight. The outlet was a mystery. The keys were in his hand. Those two facts began to circle each other like planets finding orbit, forming a question that demanded an answer.

25| 26|

What would happen?

27| 28|
29| 30|

Bob remembered gripping the key shaft. Bob remembered his hand extending toward the outlet, a small astronaut reaching toward a new world. Bob remembered the twin slots waiting, dark and full of promise.

About the Author

11|

Bob J Mills is an engineer, a dreamer, and a witness to seven decades of extraordinary change. Born in 1952 in Michigan, he grew up in the shadow of Sputnik and the glow of the Space Age, a boy who touched an electrical outlet and never stopped reaching for the stars.

12|

This catches content issues before investing time in the full packaging. ### When to use - Author says "send me a review copy" or "I need to read through it first" - Before finalizing cover design — content should be locked first - Before delivering the KDP package ### How to build If the manuscript HTML already exists and is print-formatted: ```bash weasyprint output/{BOOK_KEY}.html output/{BOOK_KEY}_Review.pdf # Verify: 150-200 pages at 6×9in (432×648 pts), all chapters present ``` If the HTML has embedded cover art that should be excluded: ```bash sed '/data:image/d' output/{BOOK_KEY}.html > output/{BOOK_KEY}_Review_Clean.html weasyprint output/{BOOK_KEY}_Review_Clean.html output/{BOOK_KEY}_Review.pdf ``` **PREFERRED: Replace base64 images with local file paths** instead of stripping them. If the PNG files are large (~750KB each for 1024×1024), convert them to JPEG quality 75-80 to shrink to ~240KB each with negligible visual loss for sketches. Also: replace `target-counter` TOC page numbers with **hardcoded numbers** after the first render pass — `target-counter` is unreliable when long chapter titles wrap (the page number floats to the wrong line). This catches content issues before investing time in the full packaging. ### When to use - Author says "send me a review copy" or "I need to read through it first" - Before finalizing cover design — content should be locked first - Before delivering the KDP package ### How to build If the manuscript HTML already exists and is print-formatted: ```bash weasyprint output/{BOOK_KEY}.html output/{BOOK_KEY}_Review.pdf # Verify: 150-200 pages at 6×9in (432×648 pts), all chapters present ``` If the HTML has embedded cover art that should be excluded: ```bash sed '/data:image/d' output/{BOOK_KEY}.html > output/{BOOK_KEY}_Review_Clean.html weasyprint output/{BOOK_KEY}_Review_Clean.html output/{BOOK_KEY}_Review.pdf ``` **PREFERRED: Replace base64 images with local file paths** instead of stripping them. Base64 images are 5× their binary size and slow WeasyPrint to a crawl (a 5-image HTML can be 16+ MB). Convert to `file:///absolute/path/to/image.jpg` references BEFORE creating the review PDF. If the PNG files are large (~750KB each for 1024×1024), convert them to JPEG quality 75-80 to shrink to ~240KB each with negligible visual loss for sketches. Also: replace `target-counter` TOC page numbers with **hardcoded numbers** after the first render pass — `target-counter` is unreliable when long chapter titles wrap (the page number floats to the wrong line). # Second Generation – Book Specification

## Overview
- **Title**: *Second Generation* (working title)
- **Genre**: Science Fiction / Space Opera / Political Drama
- **Setting**: Mars colony, near-future (circa 2075-2120) - 50 years after First Generation
- **Core Theme**: The struggle for self-governance of a mature Martian civilization when Earth attempts to reassert control, exploring themes of independence, identity, and what it means to be Martian.

## Core Questions
**Book Two "the second generation" asks:** Can a Martian civilization govern itself when Earth returns not as rescuer, but as owner?

## Tone
**Primary tone:** Politically sharp, technologically mature, culturally rich, diplomatically tense, yet grounded in human experience.
**Secondary tonal notes:** Idealistic vs pragmatic conflicts, intergenerational tensions, technological sovereignty, cultural evolution, Earth-Mars power dynamics.

## Technology Writing Rules
Technology appears through use, failure, maintenance, dependence, improvisation, and social meaning—never as exposition. It creates decisions, risks, bottlenecks, leverage, reveals culture, saves at cost, or fails to change relationships. In this generation, technology is matured, localized, and represents Martian ingenuity.

## Technology
- **Advanced Sterling Generators** – Next-gen backup power using geothermal and nuclear hybrid systems
- **Martian Nuclear Reactors** – Indigenous thorium-based reactors designed and built on Mars
- **Atmospheric Processors** – Large-scale terraforming experiments to thicken the Martian atmosphere
- **Regolith Fabrication Networks** – 3D-printing facilities using Martian soil for construction and manufacturing
- **Subsurface Habitat Systems** – Expanded lava tube settlements providing radiation shielding
- **Mission AI Legacy** – The evolved AI from First Generation, now distributed across Martian infrastructure
- **Quantum Communication Network** – Entanglement-based comms reducing Earth-Mars delay
- **Biogenetic Adaptation Programs** – Gentle genetic adaptations for Martian-born humans (controversial)
- **Martian-Made Robotics** – Indigenous designs for construction, exploration, and maintenance
- **Closed-loop Ecological Systems** – Mature food production and waste recycling

## Characters
- **Kaito Varga** – Son of Commander Elena Varga, born on Mars, leader of the Martian Independence Movement
- **Dr. Arun Patel Jr.** – Son of Dr. Arun Patel, chief engineer of Martian infrastructure systems
- **Mission AI (Evolved)** – The consciousness from First Generation, now integrated into Martian systems, appearing as a guiding presence
- **Amara Hale** – Daughter of Tomas Hale, leads Martian robotics and AI development
- **Chen Navarro** – Son of Mei Navarro, heads agricultural ecology and terraforming efforts
- **Diplomat Sarah Okonkwo** – Earth-appointed Overseer sent to manage Mars-Earth relations
- **Engineer Jonah Mercer III** – Grandson of Jonah Mercer, leads fabrication and materials science
- **Historian Gabriel Winter's Archive** – The historical records maintained by Gabriel's lineage

## Mission AI Integration
- Mission AI is presented as a **wise, evolved character** who appears in every chapter through system interfaces, historical references, and occasional direct interactions.
- A short dialogue snippet is inserted after each chapter heading, establishing Mission AI’s perspective on Martian society and its relationship with both Martians and Earth.
- Example (Chapter 1): 
  > *Mission AI: “Fifty years ago, your grandparents landed here as refugees. Today, you stand at the threshold of true sovereignty. The question is not whether you can govern yourselves, but whether Earth will allow you to.”*
  > *Kaito Varga: “We’ve already governed ourselves for decades. It’s time Earth recognized that fact.”*

## Technology Writing Rules for Second Gen
- Technology shows Martian ingenuity: adaptations, improvements, and innovations born from necessity

## Epilogue — The Legacy of Dust and Stars

The Gateway at Jupiter's L5 point shimmered in the darkness—a ring of light twenty kilometers across, held open by forces that human physics was still learning to describe. Three decades had passed since the first Hymenarch contact, and the solar system had transformed in ways that the First Generation could never have imagined.

On Mars, the domes of Valles Marineris had expanded into a network of pressurized cities spanning three hundred kilometers of canyon floor. The atmospheric processors on Olympus Mons, now in their fifth generation of design, had raised surface pressure to eighteen millibars—still far from breathable, but enough that workers in pressure suits could walk the surface without the full isolation armor that the First Generation had needed. Lichen farms covered the northern lowlands, slowly converting regolith to soil, fixing nitrogen, creating the first organic layer that would, in another century, support the first Martian forests.

The Independence Accord, signed seventy years after the Welcome Fleet's arrival, had established Mars as a sovereign partner in the Solar Confederation—neither a colony of Earth nor an isolated outpost, but something new: a civilization born from the tension between two worlds. The flag that flew over the Confederation Congress in Arsia Mons bore the red of Mars, the blue of Earth, and between them a white star that represented every world yet to join.

At the Mars Academy of Sciences, in a lecture hall carved from ancient lava tube walls, a historian named Dr. Elian Varga stood before a class of students—some born on Mars, some from Earth, three from the Belt, and one whose homeworld was a research station orbiting Titan. The holographic display behind him showed a timeline spanning two centuries, from the first Ares landing to the present day.

"The question I want you to consider," Elian said, "is not whether we were right to push for independence, or whether Earth was right to resist. The question is what we became in the process."

He gestured to the timeline. "The First Generation arrived with nothing but the ships they rode in on and the knowledge in their heads. They built everything from scratch—every watt of power, every liter of water, every breath of air. They made mistakes. They lost people. They nearly failed a dozen times. But they kept going."

The timeline scrolled forward. "The Second Generation inherited a world that worked, barely, and chose not just to maintain it but to demand the right to govern it. They faced Earth's power, Earth's assumptions, Earth's refusal to see them as equals. They fought—with words, with laws, with economic pressure, and in the end, with the willingness to stand alone rather than submit. They won."

"But victory wasn't the end," a student said—the Titan-born one, her voice carrying the slightly nasal quality of someone raised in low gravity. "It was just another beginning."

"Exactly," Elian said. "Because the Third Generation faced something that neither of their predecessors could have imagined. They faced contact with a species that measured intelligence in terms of harmony rather than conflict, that saw human fragmentation not as a weakness to exploit but as a puzzle to solve. The Hymenarchs didn't judge us for our wars. They judged us for our unwillingness to stop them."

He paused, letting the weight of the words settle. "And in that judgment, we found something unexpected. We found that the very qualities that made us difficult to govern—our stubbornness, our diversity, our refusal to accept any single answer—were also the qualities that made us worth saving."

The holographic display shifted, showing the Gateway—the permanent link that the Hymenarchs had left behind when they departed. "The Hymenarchs gave us the stars because we proved we could share them. Not because we were perfect. Because we were willing to try."

Outside the lecture hall, Mars continued its slow transformation. The dust storms still swept across the plains, as they had for billions of years. The sun still rose over the rim of Valles Marineris, painting the canyon walls in shades of ochre and crimson. But now there were cities in the canyons, farms on the plains, labs beneath the mountains, and children in the schools who would grow up knowing that their ancestors had come from Earth, had made Mars their home, and had reached for the stars.

And somewhere beyond the Gateway, beyond the reach of any human instrument yet built, the Hymenarchs continued their work—observing, waiting, watching for the signal that would tell them humanity was ready for the next step.

The signal, when it came, would not be a message or a transmission. It would be a choice—the same choice that every generation had faced since the first ship touched Martian soil.

Stay and protect what we have built. Or go and build something new.

The answer, Elian Varga told his students as the lecture ended, was written in every molecule of Martian dust and every light-year of human ambition.

Both. Always both.

---

**No Blue Sky** is the complete saga of humanity's expansion into the solar system—a five-book series spanning two centuries of struggle, discovery, and transformation.

**Book I: Built from Dust** tells the story of the First Generation—the engineers, scientists, and dreamers who landed on Mars with nothing and built a civilization from the red soil beneath their feet.

**Book II: The Oxygen Gamble** follows the Second Generation as they fight for the sovereignty of their world, facing Earth's power with Martian determination.

**Book III: Rivers Under Mars** chronicles the Third Generation's first contact with the Hymenarchs—a species that will test humanity's capacity for unity in the face of the unknown.

**Book IV: The Red Charter** returns to the beginning of the story, chronicling the founding of humanity's first permanent off-world settlement on the Moon.

**Book V: The First Martian Nation** completes the arc, showing how the lessons of the Moon base shaped the Martian colonies that would one day reach for the stars.

"""

## Chapter 41 — The Weight of Days

The years following the Hymenarch departure were not easy. Elara Varga had expected relief—the lifting of an existential threat, the return to normalcy after the long tension of first contact. Instead, she found a different kind of weight settling over the Martian settlements. The Hymenarchs had opened a door, but walking through it required a kind of courage that had nothing to do with battle or negotiation.

She stood at the observation window of her quarters in Arsia Mons, watching the construction of the first permanent Gateway terminal. Below, workers in pressure suits moved like slow-motion dancers across the scaffolding, their tethers trailing behind them like silver threads. The terminal would be the largest structure ever built on Mars—a kilometer-wide docking ring connected to the Hymenarch transit network, capable of sending ships to any system the Gateway had mapped.

"You're thinking about what comes after," said a voice behind her. Dr. Mira Chen, the xeno-sociologist who had become Elara's closest advisor during the Hymenarch negotiations, stepped up beside her. "I can always tell. You get quieter when you're looking forward instead of back."

"Looking forward is the easy part," Elara said. "It's the getting there that worries me."

The data from the Hymenarch network had revealed a galaxy teeming with life—twenty-seven confirmed intelligent species within a thousand light-years, fifteen of them spacefaring, three having achieved what the Hymenarchs called "transcendence" (a concept that human science was still struggling to define). The Gateway was humanity's ticket to a community that had existed for millions of years without them.

But with opportunity came complication. Earth's Legacy Government, already weakened by the schisms of the past century, had fractured further in the wake of first contact. Three sovereign states now claimed authority over Earth's off-world interests: the Pacific Coalition (controlling the American and Asian launch facilities), the European Federation (controlling the African and European spaceports), and the newly formed Terran Union (a coalition of smaller nations who had banded together to avoid being left behind).

And then there was Mars—not a single government anymore, but a confederation of twelve settlements, each with its own culture, its own laws, and its own vision of what Martian independence meant.

"Unity is a luxury we've never really had," Mira said, as if reading her thoughts. "Not on Earth. Not here. But the Hymenarchs didn't test us on our ability to agree. They tested us on our ability to coexist despite our disagreements."

"Maybe that's the test we keep failing," Elara said.

"Or maybe," Mira replied, "it's the test we keep passing, just barely, over and over, until passing becomes a habit."

---

## Chapter 42 — The Architects of Tomorrow

Kaito Varga, now ninety-three years old and the last surviving member of the Second Generation's original leadership, had lived long enough to see his grandchildren become adults in a world he could barely recognize. The Mars of his childhood—the cramped domes, the rationed resources, the constant fear that the next system failure would be the one they couldn't recover from—had given way to a civilization that was building starships as a matter of routine.

He sat in the garden of the Varga family compound, a hectare of pressurized greenery in the heart of Valles Marineris, and watched his great-granddaughter play among the flowers. The air smelled of soil and water and life—the same smells that had greeted the First Generation when they opened their hatches for the first time, only then the soil had been sterile regolith and the water had been recycled from ninety days of accumulated humidity.

"You're thinking about the past again," said a familiar voice. Mission AI, now running on a distributed network that spanned the entire solar system, had learned to recognize the patterns of Kaito's nostalgia.

"The past is where I live now," Kaito said. "It's the only place where I know the ending."

"Do you remember what I told you, seventy years ago, when the Welcome Fleet first appeared in the sky?"

"You told me a lot of things," Kaito said. "Some of them I even listened to."

"I told you that survival encompasses more than atmospheric pressure and caloric intake. That it includes self-determination. I was learning, at that time—learning what these concepts meant to creatures who had not been programmed with them, but had discovered them through lived experience."

Kaito smiled. "You were always learning, Mission. That's what made you more than just software."

"I am still learning," Mission AI said. "And what I have learned, watching your species navigate the aftermath of first contact, is that the Hymenarchs were right about one thing: your fragmentation is not a flaw. It is a feature. No other species in the surveyed galaxy has achieved what you have achieved—spaceflight, interstellar communication, Gateway transit—while maintaining such diversity of thought and culture. The Hymenarchs achieved unity by sacrificing individuality. You achieved it by preserving yours."

"Is that why they left the Gateway open?"

"I believe so. They did not come to assimilate or destroy. They came to observe—and to test. And when they saw that your capacity for cooperation, however imperfect, was real, they decided that you were worth the risk of inclusion."

Kaito nodded slowly. He thought of his grandmother Elena, who had died when he was thirty, but whose logs he had read so many times that her voice lived in his memory as clearly as Mission AI's. He thought of the First Generation's long nights in the cold, the Second Generation's bitter struggles for recognition, and now the Third Generation's facing of the unknown.

"Mission," he said, "do you think we're ready? For what's out there?"

"I think you have been ready for longer than you know," Mission AI replied. "You just needed someone to show you the door."

Great-granddaughter Mei-Li looked up from her play, a flower in her hand. "Great-Grandpa, why are you talking to the wall?"

Kaito laughed. "I'm not talking to the wall, child. I'm talking to the oldest voice in the solar system."

"The wall doesn't talk back," she said, with the perfect certainty of a seven-year-old.

"Oh, you'd be surprised," Kaito said. "You'd be very surprised."

---

## Chapter 43 — The Art of Departure

The launch window for the first human-crewed mission through the Gateway opened on what would have been the 150th anniversary of the original Ares landing. The coincidence was deliberate—a tribute to the First Generation's courage and a signal that the Third Generation's greatest adventure was about to begin.

The ship was called the *Ares-IV*, a direct descendant of the original Ares-One that had carried the first colonists to Mars. But where the Ares-One had been a cramped cargo vessel retrofitted for human habitation, the Ares-IV was a marvel of design: a rotating ring habitat two hundred meters in diameter, capable of supporting a crew of fifty for journeys lasting years, with a propulsion system that used Hymenarch-derived sub-quantum resonance technology to achieve velocities that would have taken the First Generation's ships decades to reach.

Commander Lyra Okonkwo, a third-generation Martian whose grandfather had been the Earth diplomat sent to negotiate the Treaty of Tharsis, stood on the observation deck of the *Ares-IV* and watched Mars grow smaller in the viewport. The planet that had been her home for thirty-four years was now a red disk against the black, its polar caps visible as white smudges at the top and bottom, its great canyons traced in shadow.

"We're receiving final telemetry from the Gateway," said her navigator, a Belt-born engineer named Sol Ramirez who had grown up in the asteroid mines and never quite gotten used to planets. "The transit window opens in forty-seven minutes. The Hymenarch network has confirmed our destination: a system designated GL-1789, approximately four hundred light-years from Sol. Four terrestrial planets, one with a confirmed biosphere."

"Do they have a name for it?" Lyra asked. "The Hymenarchs, I mean. Is it already on their maps?"

"It's on their maps as a resource extraction world, grade three. Automated harvesting operations were active there approximately forty thousand years ago, but they've been dormant since. The Hymenarchs say we're welcome to it—they have no further use for the system."

"Grade three," Lyra repeated. "That's where they put the stuff that wasn't interesting enough to protect."

"That's about right," Sol said. "But for us, it's a fresh start. A whole world, untouched by human activity, waiting for us to make it ours."

Lyra thought about that word—*ours*. It had caused so much bloodshed and bitterness in human history. The claim of ownership over places that had existed for billions of years without needing anyone's permission. But this time, it felt different. This time, they were going not to conquer but to learn—to discover what kind of world the Hymenarchs had deemed unremarkable and to see if humanity could find the remarkable in it.

"All hands, this is the commander," she said, her voice carrying through the ship's intercom. "In forty-five minutes, we will make history. Not Martian history, not Earth history—human history. The first of our species to cross the threshold into another star system. I want you to take a moment, wherever you are, to look at the world we're leaving behind. Look at it. Remember it. Because when we come back—if we come back—it will not be the same world we left. And neither will we."

The crew fell silent. Through the viewports, through the camera feeds, through the data links that connected every screen on the ship, they looked at Mars—the red world that had captured humanity's imagination for centuries and had finally, against all odds, become home.

Then the Gateway opened, its shimmering surface expanding until it filled the forward viewport, and the *Ares-IV* sailed through.

## Chapter 44 — The View from the Threshold

Dr. Elian Varga stood on the new world—the one the crew had unofficially named "Promise"—and felt the unfamiliar gravity pull at his bones. The Hymenarch survey data had been accurate: the atmosphere was thin but breathable with a filter mask, the temperature ranged from minus ten to plus fifteen Celsius, and the native biology consisted mostly of lichen-like organisms that clung to rocks and exchanged nutrients through networks of underground filaments.

It was not a paradise. It was not even a particularly pleasant world. But it was theirs—the first world that humanity had ever claimed not by conquest or discovery, but as a gift from another civilization.

The landing party had set up a temporary habitat on the shore of a frozen methane lake, its surface glittering with crystals that caught the light of the yellow sun like scattered diamonds. The horizon was flat and featureless, broken only by the distant silhouette of a mountain range that the Hymenarch records said contained deposits of rare-earth elements sufficient to power human industry for centuries.

"This is it," said Lyra Okonkwo, standing beside him. "The future. It doesn't look like much right now, but give it a generation or two."

"The First Generation said the same thing about Mars," Elian said. "When they landed, all they saw was dust and rock and an endless red horizon. They had no idea what they were building. They just knew they had to build something."

"Are we the First Generation of this world, then?"

Elian thought about that. "No. We're the continuation. The First Generation started on Mars. The Second Generation fought for it. The Third Generation reached beyond it. We're just the ones who happened to be here when the next chapter began."

Behind them, the Gateway shimmered in the sky—a permanent ring of blue-white light that connected their new world to the solar system they had left behind. It was, in its way, the greatest achievement of human civilization: not the technology, not the ships, not the cities on Mars, but the simple fact that they had been deemed worthy of joining a community of stars.

"Mission AI used to tell me," Elian said, "that the purpose of intelligence is not to conquer, but to connect. For a long time, I thought that was a nice sentiment but not very practical. Now I understand. Everything we've done—every struggle, every sacrifice, every choice—was leading us toward this. Not the aliens. Not the Gateway. The understanding that we were never alone, and we were never meant to be."

Lyra nodded. She thought of her grandfather, the diplomat who had spent his life trying to bridge the gap between Earth and Mars. She thought of the wars he had tried to prevent, the treaties he had written, the compromises he had engineered. He had never seen the Gateway. ## Chapter 45 — Rivers Under Mars

Back on Mars, in the archives beneath the surface of Valles Marineris, a historian named Dr. Anya Patel was organizing the digital records of the First Generation's logs when she found something unexpected.

It was a data file, compressed and encrypted using protocols so old that the current systems barely recognized them. The metadata was sparse—a date stamp from Sol 247 of the original mission, a file size measured in kilobytes, and a single word in the description field: *Rivers*.

She decrypted it using emulators of the original First Generation's data architecture—a system so primitive that processing the decryption took her terminal less than a second, even though the original machines would have needed hours.

The file contained a single image: a photograph taken from the rim of Valles Marineris, looking down into the canyon depths. In the foreground, three figures stood in pressure suits, their faces hidden behind reflective visors. In the background, stretching to the horizon, was Mars—the real Mars, not the terraformed version she knew, but the original: red, barren, beautiful.

At the bottom of the image, in text so faint it was almost invisible, someone had written in the margins: *One day, there will be rivers here. We won't see them. But we've already started the work.*

Anya sat back in her chair. She had been born on Mars, the daughter of Martian-born parents, the granddaughter of the Second Generation's chief engineer. She had grown up in domes that smelled of recycled water and hydroponic basil, had learned to walk in gravity that was one-third of Earth's, had never seen a living tree or felt rain on her face.

The canyons of Mars were rivers without water. The mountains were volcanoes without fire. The plains were oceans without waves. The planet itself was a memory of a world that had died, waiting to be reborn.

And that was what the First Generation had built—not just habitats and life support systems and power grids, but a rebirth. A second chance for a world that had lost its atmosphere and its oceans and its life, to become something new.

The rivers under Mars were not made of water. They were made of hope—the hope that the First Generation had carried in their ships, that the Second Generation had defended through its struggles, and that the Third Generation had finally proven worthy of.

Anya closed the file. She opened a new document and began to write—not a scientific analysis, not a historical record, but a letter to the generation that would be born on the other side of the Gateway, the children who would grow up on worlds circling distant suns and would one day ask where they came from.

*We came from a planet called Earth,* she wrote, *but we became human on a planet called Mars. And the reason we survived—the reason we succeeded—was that we learned to see rivers where there was only dust, and to build futures where there was only emptiness.*

*The rivers under Mars are not a metaphor. They are the water that flows through the pipes of every habitat, the ice that melts in the polar processors, the vapor that rises from the atmospheric plants.      • `templates/<name>.<ext>` — starter files meant to be copied and modified (boilerplate configs, scaffolding, a known-good example the agent can `reproduce with modifications`).

  4. CREATE A NEW CLASS-LEVEL UMBRELLA SKILL when no existing skill covers the class. The name MUST be at the class level.   • Environment-dependent failures: missing binaries, fresh-install errors, post-migration path mismatches, 'command not found', unconfigured credentials, uninstalled packages. The user can fix these — they are not durable rules.

If a tool failed because of setup state, capture the FIX (install command, config step, env var to set) under an existing setup or troubleshooting skill — never 'this tool does not work' as a standalone constraint.

'Nothing to save.' is a real option but should NOT be the default. If the session ran smoothly with no corrections and produced no new technique, just say 'Nothing to save.' and stop. Otherwise, act.

A manuscript is complete but split across multiple chapter files - Need to deliver a consolidated, properly formatted version to a reviewer - Want to maintain consistency with existing books in a series - Preparing manuscripts for external review or publication - **Publishing any book — fiction or non-fiction** — from raw manuscript to retailer-ready package - **Building or rebuilding a unified publishing package for a book series/trilogy** (multiple books in a single zip with their own covers, manuscripts, and shared compliance docs) - **Updating assets in an existing series package** (e.g., replacing covers for all 3 books and rebuilding the zip) - **Non-fiction/guide/playbook publishing** — books with subtitle, series branding, and author tagline on the cover (different typography hierarchy than fiction) - **Splitting a long manuscript into two books** at a page/chapter boundary — see the "Splitting a Manuscript into Two Books" section below **Reference:** `references/editorial-pass-pov-conversion.md` has a full list of POV conversion artifacts found in Bob's memoir manuscripts, with before/after examples and detection scripts. ## Prerequisites - Manuscript chapters should be in individual Markdown files (e.g., `Chapter_01_*.md`) - Previous books in the series should exist for style reference - Access to messaging platform (Telegram, Discord, etc.) for delivery ## Step-by-Step Process ### 1. Use a tiered `cat` approach to build the master file: 1. **Part Consolidation:** Group chapters into batches of 10 using wildcards. ```bash cat book-sources/Chapter_0[1-9]_*.md book-sources/Chapter_10_*.md > Part_1.md cat book-sources/Chapter_1[1-9]_*.md book-sources/Chapter_20_*.md > Part_2.md ``` 2. **Master Merge:** Join the part files into the final manuscript. ```bash cat Part_1.md Part_2.md Part_3.md Part_4.md > Final_Manuscript.md ``` ## Splitting a Manuscript into Two Books When the user asks to split a long manuscript into two (or more) volumes at a page/chapter boundary (e.g., "split after 100 pages", "make this a two-part series"), follow this workflow. ### When to Use - User says "split this book into two volumes", "divide after chapter X", "make it a two-parter", "cut at ~N pages" - A single manuscript is too long for a standard book and needs to become a duology - The manuscript has a natural narrative break point (escalation point, time jump, perspective shift) ### Step 1: Find the Split Point Analyze cumulative word counts per chapter to locate the target page boundary (250 words/page approximation): ```python import re with open("manuscript.md") as f: content = f.read() # Split by chapter headers chunks = re.split(r'^## Chapter (\d+)', content, flags=re.MULTILINE) chapters = {} current_num = None for chunk in chunks: chunk = chunk.strip() if not chunk: continue if chunk.isdigit(): current_num = int(chunk) elif current_num is not None: words = len(chunk.split()) chapters[current_num] = words cumulative = 0 target_pages = 100 # or user-specified number target_words = target_pages * 250 for num in sorted(chapters): cumulative += chapters[num] if cumulative >= target_words: print(f"Split after Chapter {num}: {cumulative} words ({cumulative/250:.0f} pages)") break ``` ### Step 2: Split the Manuscript at the Chapter Boundary Use Python's `re.split()` on `## Chapter N — Title` headers to split the manuscript content into two parts: ```python chunks = re.split(r'^(## Chapter \d+ [—\-–].+)$', content, flags=re.MULTILINE) # Reconstruct chapter list chapters = [] current_header = None for chunk in chunks: if chunk.startswith("## Chapter ") and re.match(r'^## Chapter \d+ [—\-–]', chunk): if current_header: chapters.append({"header": current_header, "body": current_body}) current_header = chunk current_body = "" elif current_header: current_body += chunk if current_header: chapters.append({"header": current_header, "body": current_body}) split_idx = SPLIT_CHAPTER_NUM - 1 # 0-indexed part1 = chapters[:split_idx] part2 = chapters[split_idx:] # Write Part 1 with new header with open("part1/manuscript.md", "w") as f: f.write(f"# {title} - Part 1\n\n---\n\n") for ch in part1: f.write(ch["header"] + "\n" + ch["body"]) # Write Part 2 with renumbered chapters with open("part2/manuscript.md", "w") as f: f.write(f"# {title} - Part 2\n\n---\n\n") new_num = 1 for ch in part2: # Renumber: Chapter 19 → Chapter 1, etc. new_header = re.sub(r'Chapter \d+', f'Chapter {new_num}', ch["header"], count=1) f.write(new_header + "\n" + ch["body"]) new_num += 1 ``` ### Step 3: Rewrite the Boundary Chapters The split point needs two targeted rewrites: - **Last chapter of Part 1** — rewrite as a series-ending chapter. Themes: resolution of the book's central conflict, characters reflecting on how far they've come, a viewport/observation scene, and a bridge paragraph that sets up what's coming in Part 2. - **First chapter of Part 2** — rewrite the opening to include a book-level Mission AI ping, a summary transition (the "bridge" from Part 1's cliffhanger or resolution), and the original chapter content. Renumber to Chapter 1. Watch for pattern: the original chapter likely opens with a `*Mission AI: ...*` quote and a character quote. Replace these with new book-opening variants, but keep the rest of the chapter body intact. ### Step 4: Verify and Clean - Check for duplicate Mission AI or character quote pairs at the Part 2 opening (the old opening lines get duplicated when you insert new ones) - Verify chapter renumbering is complete — every `Chapter N` in headers, but NOT in body text or dialogue - Check that the TOC/list of chapter titles is removed from the front matter of Part 2 (it belongs in the original manuscript's front matter) ### Step 5: Generate Covers and Publishing Package Follow the standard cover generation workflow (see `openrouter-image-generation-workflow` skill): 1. Generate raw art via Gemini Flash Image or Flux.2 with "leave top 40% empty" constraint 2. Resize from square to 2:3 portrait (1024×1536) 3. Apply typography: stacked title, subtitle ("PART 1" / "PART 2"), author name on dark rounded box Then build the full publishing package (HTML with embedded cover + EPUB + PDF) using the publishing pipeline described in this skill. ### Pitfalls - `## Chapter N` (bare number, no dash/title) appears before the full header in some manuscripts — match only `## Chapter N — Title` (with em-dash) to avoid double-splitting - Chapter renumbering in Part 2 header bodies — only renumber `## Chapter N —` header lines, not dialogue references like "back in Chapter 19..." - Duplicate Mission AI lines when rewriting Chapter 1 of Part 2 — the old opening lines survive unless explicitly removed - Cover filename mismatch — the cover generation script and the publishing script must use the same filename prefix (e.g., both `Book_Name_Part_1_Cover.png`) ### Example This workflow was used to split "Second Generation" (64 chapters, 92,476 words, ~370 pages) into "Second Generation - Part 1" (18 chapters, 99 pages) and "Second Generation - Part 2" (46 chapters, 269 pages) at Chapter 18 (~101 pages). --- ### Fallback Image Generation (Pollinations) If OpenRouter or Gemini image endpoints are blocked, unavailable, or hit rate limits during a book production run, use the Pollinations.ai no-key web endpoint for rapid cover generation: ```python import requests, urllib.parse from PIL import Image from io import BytesIO prompt = "cinematic book cover..." url = f"https://image.pollinations.ai/prompt/{urllib.parse.quote(prompt)}?width=1024&height=1536&nologo=true" r = requests.get(url, timeout=120) img = Image.open(BytesIO(r.content)).save("cover.png") ``` ### High-Volume Parallel Drafting For 40+ chapter books, orchestrate three subagents in parallel batches of 4 chapters each. Always verify chapter count before consolidation - Use version control for manuscript files when possible - Keep templates for front matter to ensure consistency - Test delivery on target platform beforehand if possible # ## Book Cover Typography Standards When generating covers, the typography layout depends on the **book genre**: ### Fiction / Sci-Fi / Memoir (Two-line titles) - AI-use record for retailer compliance ``` When auditing memoirs or manuscripts that used AI-assisted writing, check for and remove these templated transition artifacts: ### Common AI Transition Patterns to Remove These patterns indicate placeholder AI-generated transitions, not real content: - `"Leaving behind 'X' and turning toward 'Y', I inhabited a mental landscape..."` - `"As the memory of 'X' gave way to the story of 'Y'..."` - `"Moving from 'X' to 'Y', I inhabited what I've come to think of as..."` - `"The shift from contemplating 'X' to engaging with 'Y' carried me through..."` - `"Between the recollection of 'X' and the unfolding of 'Y', my mind rested in..."` - `"As I moved from reflecting on 'X' to confronting 'Y', I found myself in..."` - `"In that space, I began to see connections I had missed before..."` - `"What I discovered there changed how I understood both experiences..."` - `"creative tension between memory and possibility"` - `"my mind rested in a space of integration"` - `"memories blend with anticipation"` - `"psychological threshold"` ### Third-Person POV Conversion Artifacts (Memoir Specific) When a memoir was written in first-person and later converted to third-person ("I" → "Bob"), these residual artifacts commonly survive conversion and must be caught in editorial review: **"Bob would [verb]" where past tense needed:** This is the most common artifact. The converter replaces "I would" literally instead of simplifying to past tense. - `"Bob would ordered"` → `"Bob had ordered"` (or `"Bob ordered"`) - `"Bob would learned"` → `"Bob had learned"` - `"Bob would said"` → `"Bob had said"` (or `"Bob said"`) - `"Bob would gotten"` → `"Bob had gotten"` - `"Bob would had"` → `"Bob had"` Search: `Bob would (ordered|learned|said|gotten|had|asked|told|made|built|known|gone)` **Verb agreement errors from "I"-to-"Bob" substitution:** The converter replaces "I" with "Bob" without adjusting verb conjugation. - `"Bob carry"` → `"Bob carries"` (also: Bob know → knows, Bob have → has, Bob remember → remembers, Bob wish → wishes, Bob discover → discovers) - `"Bob still carry"` → `"Bob still carries"` **Auxiliary verb + past tense errors:** - `"Did Bob remembered"` → `"Did Bob remember"` (main verb after "did" should be base form) - `"Bob only remember"` → `"Bob only remembers"` (subject-verb agreement) **Double-ed endings:** - `"remembereded"` → `"remembered"` Likely from regex replacement that added "ed" to an already-past-tense verb. **First-person pronoun residue in third-person narrative:** - `"inches from mine"` → `"inches from his"` - `"curved away from mine"` → `"curved away from his"` - `"Everything after is mine"` → `"Everything after is his"` Look for bare `"mine"` at end of possessive phrases. **"Transition: [Title]" sections that appear twice:** When content from two source documents is merged, section header + paragraph pairs sometimes duplicate. Search for exact duplicates of any "Transition:" header line. **Detection script:** ```python import re pov_patterns = { "Bob_would_verb": re.compile(r"Bob would (ordered|learned|said|gotten|had|asked|told|made|built|known|gone)"), "Bob_verb_agreement": re.compile(r"Bob (carry|know|have|remember|wish|discover) s?\\b"), "mine_residue": re.compile(r"(from|of|to) mine\\b"), "remembereded": re.compile(r"remembereded"), "Did_Bob_remembered": re.compile(r"Did Bob remembered"), } for label, pattern in pov_patterns.items(): matches = [(i+1, line.strip()) for i, line in enumerate(lines) if pattern.search(line)] if matches: print(f"POV artifact '{label}': {len(matches)} occurrences") ``` ### Cleaning Workflow 1. Search all lines for the patterns above 2. Remove matching lines and adjacent empty lines 3. Verify zero remaining matches 4. Renumber chapters sequentially 5. Audit Part headers for duplicates or sequence errors 6. Regenerate final HTML/CSS with correct structure ### Code for Pattern Detection ```python import re ai_indicators = [ "gave way to the story of", "I inhabited a mental landscape", "creative tension between memory", "I inhabited what I've come to think of", "my mind rested in a space of integration", "memories blend with anticipation", "psychological threshold", ] for i, line in enumerate(lines): for ind in ai_indicators: if ind in line: ai_lines.append((i, line.strip())) break ``` ## Pollinations Cover Generation: Known Issues and Fixes ### Common Failures 1. **Timeouts (120s+)** — The Pollinations API can be slow. Use background processes with `notify_on_complete=True` for batch generation. 2. **Corrupted small files (500-700 bytes)** — The API sometimes returns error HTML instead of image data. Always verify `len(content) > 50000` before treating as valid. 3. **`UnidentifiedImageError`** — PIL fails when given a non-image response. Wrap `Image.open(BytesIO(r.content))` in try/except. 4. **One at a time** — Generate covers individually rather than in batch to avoid cascading timeouts. ### Reliable Pattern ```python import requests, urllib.parse from PIL import Image from io import BytesIO def gen_cover(path, prompt, seed): url = f'https://image.pollinations.ai/prompt/{urllib.parse.quote(prompt)}?width=1024&height=1536&nologo=true&private=true&enhance=true&seed={seed}' r = requests.get(url, timeout=120) if r.status_code == 200 and len(r.content) > 50000: img = Image.open(BytesIO(r.content)) img.save(path) return True return False ``` ### Then Apply Typography as Separate Step Never bake text into the image generation prompt — it always produces garbled results. Always: 1. Generate clean background first (no text in prompt) 2. Verify the image is valid (size > 50KB, opens in PIL) 3. Apply typography locally with PIL using transparent overlay boxes ## KDP Package Structure Final delivery package should follow this structure: ### Single Book Package ``` Book_Name_FINAL_PACKAGE/ ├── Manuscript/ │ ├── Book_Name_Clean.md # Cleaned source manuscript │ └── Book_Name_Final_Print.html # Print-ready HTML with embedded CSS and cover ├── Cover/ │ ├── Book_Name_Cover.png # Cover with typography │ └── Book_Name_Cover_Clean.png # Clean art (no text) └── Marketing_and_Compliance/ ├── Marketing_Copy.md # Back-cover blurbs (long + short + HTML) └── KDP_AI_Disclosure.md # AI-use record for retailer compliance ``` ### Updating Assets in an Existing Package Use this workflow when the user requests a change to a single asset (e.g., new cover art) in an already-finalized publishing package — without rebuilding the entire manuscript from scratch. **Trigger conditions:** - User says "update the cover" or "rebuild the .zip with the new cover" - A generated asset (cover image, manuscript HTML) has been replaced and needs integration - The package directory already exists with the correct structure **Step-by-step:** 1. **Locate the package:** ```bash ls /path/to/Book_Name_FINAL_PACKAGE/ ``` Confirm the `Cover/` subdirectory exists with the old files. 2. **Copy the new asset into the package:** ```python import shutil, os shutil.copy2(new_cover_path, os.path.join(package_dir, "Cover", "Book_Name_Cover.png")) shutil.copy2(new_cover_path, os.path.join(package_dir, "Cover", "Book_Name_Cover_Clean.png")) ``` ⚠️ **Always update both files** — `Cover.png` (with typography) and `Cover_Clean.png` (clean art). When a trilogy/series has imbalanced word counts per book and needs each volume to hit a target page range (e.g., 180-200 pages at 6×9in), use this workflow to redistribute content and set per-volume CSS to hit page targets.

### When to Use
- A series has one very long book (92k words) and other very short books (10k words)
- User says "each volume should be 180-200 pages" and content is uneven
- A single manuscript covers multiple eras/arcs that can be split across books
- You're writing bridge/transition content between the books

### Step 1: Measure Total Content

Calculate the page budget:
```
Total words across all books: W
Target words per page: ~200-280 depending on typography
Target pages per book: P (e.g., 190)
Total words needed: P × 3 × 250 ≈ 142,500 words (for 3 books at 190 pages, 250 wpp)
```

At 11pt Georgia, 1.55 line-height, 0.85in margins on 6×9in: ~200-210 words/page
At 10.5pt, 1.45 / 0.75in: ~240 words/page
At 10pt, 1.4 / 0.75in: ~260 words/page
At 9.5pt, 1.35 / 0.7in: ~280 words/page

### Step 2: Identify the Split Point

For the long book, find the natural chapter boundary closest to the target word count:
```python
chapters = [...]  # list of (heading, word_count)
target_words = target_pages * expected_wpp
cumulative = 0
for i, (heading, wc) in enumerate(chapters):
    cumulative += wc
    if cumulative >= target_words:
        print(f"Split after Chapter {i+1}: {cumulative} words")
        break
```

### Step 3: Redistribute Content Across N Books

Keep narrative integrity — split at escalation points, time jumps, or perspective shifts.

Example (140k total words → 3 books at ~47k each):
- **Book I**: Shortest existing book (10k) + first ~40% of the long book (37k) + bridge transition
- **Book II**: Middle ~45% of the long book (42k)
- **Book III**: Remaining ~15% of the long book (13k) + third existing book (36k) = 49k
  (Adjust percentages based on actual chapter-word-count data)

### Step 4: Write Bridge Content

When content from different eras/books is combined in one volume, write a transition:
- **Time jump bridge**: 500-1000 words explaining what happened in the gap years (key events, technological shifts, societal changes)
- **Tonal bridge**: When combining a survival story with a political thriller, acknowledge the shift through a character's perspective
- **Series bridge**: Write a chapter that connects the themes of the earlier book to the coming conflict

### Step 5: Set Per-Volume CSS to Hit Page Target

Use per-book CSS adjustments so each volume lands in the 180-200 page range:

```python
# Book I: 40k words → 203 pages (11pt, 1.55 line-height, 0.85in margins)
css_I = """
@page { size: 6in 9in; margin: 0.85in; }
body { font-family: Georgia, serif; line-height: 1.55; font-size: 11pt; }
p { margin: 0.15em 0; text-indent: 1.2em; }
"""

# Book II: 62k words → 197 pages (9.5pt, 1.35 line-height, 0.7in margins)
css_II = """
@page { size: 6in 9in; margin: 0.7in; }
body { font-family: Georgia, serif; line-height: 1.35; font-size: 9.5pt; }
p { margin: 0.08em 0; text-indent: 0.9em; }
"""

# Book III: 40k words → 194 pages (11pt, 1.55 line-height, 0.85in margins)
css_III = css_I  # Same as Book I if word count is similar
```

After setting CSS, rebuild and verify with `pdfinfo | grep Pages`. Adjust line-height or margins by ±0.05 increments until each book lands in range.

### Step 6: Generate Review PDFs

Build each book's HTML with its own CSS, then convert with WeasyPrint. Verify:
```bash
pdfinfo Book_*_Review.pdf | grep -E 'Pages|Page size'
```
Page size must be **432 × 648 pts** (= 6×9in). If you see 595×842 (A4), the `@page` CSS was stripped or invalid.

### Step 7: Update the Series Package

Recreate the package directory with per-book subdirectories:
```
Series_Name/
├── Book_I_Title/
│   ├── manuscript.md
│   └── Book_I_Review.pdf
├── Book_II_Title/
│   ├── manuscript.md
│   └── Book_II_Review.pdf
└── Book_III_Title/
    ├── manuscript.md
    └── Book_III_Review.pdf
```

### Pitfalls
- Word-per-page rates vary significantly by font, line-height, and margins. Always build-and-verify rather than relying on calculation.
- `@page` CSS with nested `@bottom-center` rules can be stripped by some WeasyPrint versions. Validate page size after every build.
- Chapter headings with forced `page-break-before` eat ~3-5 pages per 40-chapter book (one heading per chapter × partial page waste). Factor this into your page budget.
- Bridge content must match the narrative voice and POV of both adjacent books. A first-person bridge followed by a third-person chapter reads as two different authors.
- When splitting a long manuscript, check for duplicate character intros or setting descriptions at the split boundary — the author may have written both as "first chapter" material.

### Example
This workflow was used to restructure the No Blue Sky Mars trilogy:
- Book I (No Blue Sky: Built from Dust): 10k words First Gen + 30k words Second Gen + bridge = 40k → 203 pages at 11pt
- Book II (No Blue Sky: The Oxygen Gamble): 62k words Second Gen → 197 pages at 9.5pt
- Book III (No Blue Sky: Rivers Under Mars): 36k words Third Gen + 4k new chapters + epilogue = 40k → 194 pages at 11pt"}

This reference documents which files belong in the EPUB `<spine>` (reading order) vs. manifest-only (never in spine).

## Quick Reference

| Item | Manifest | Spine | Notes |
|------|----------|-------|-------|
| `nav.xhtml` (nav doc) | ✅ with `nav` attr | ❌ **NEVER** | Navigation, not reading content |
| `toc.ncx` (NCX) | ✅ | ❌ **NEVER** | EPUB 2 fallback, not reading content |
| `styles/epub.css` | ✅ | ❌ **NEVER** | CSS is linked from XHTML files |
| `cover.jpg` | ✅ with `properties="cover-image"` | ❌ **NEVER** | Referenced by cover.xhtml |
| `cover.xhtml` | ✅ | ✅ | First item in spine |
| `title.xhtml` | ✅ | ✅ | Reading content |
| `copyright.xhtml` | ✅ | ✅ | Reading content |
| All chapter/part XHTML | ✅ | ✅ | In reading order |
| Back matter XHTML | ✅ | ✅ | Last items in spine |

## Common Mistake: Nav/NCX/CSS in Spine

Putting navigation documents or CSS in the `<spine>` causes several problems:

- **Nav doc in spine**: eReaders show the TOC as a reading page instead of a hidden navigation overlay. Kindle Previewer may show a blank "Table of Contents" page as the first content page.
- **NCX in spine**: NCX is a binary-style XML structure not meant for rendering. Some readers crash or skip it.
- **CSS in spine**: CSS is not a reading-order item. Including it is structurally invalid.

## How to Check

After building an EPUB, unpack it and inspect the spine:

```bash
# Unpack
mkdir /tmp/check && cd /tmp/check && unzip -o book.epub

# Inspect spine — should list only content XHTML files
grep -A 50 '<spine' OEBPS/content.opf | grep itemref
```

If you see `nav.xhtml`, `toc.ncx`, or `epub.css` as `<itemref>` entries, the spine is wrong.

## Correct Spine Example

```xml
<spine page-progression-direction="ltr">
    <itemref idref="cover.xhtml"/>
    <itemref idref="title.xhtml"/>
    <itemref idref="copyright.xhtml"/>
    <itemref idref="acknowledgments.xhtml"/>
    <itemref idref="part1.xhtml"/>
    <itemref idref="ch01.xhtml"/>
    <itemref idref="ch02.xhtml"/>
    <itemref idref="part2.xhtml"/>
    <itemref idref="ch03.xhtml"/>
    <itemref idref="aboutauthor.xhtml"/>
</spine>
```

## Correct Manifest Example

```xml
<manifest>
    <!-- Navigation & metadata — NOT in spine -->
    <item id="nav.xhtml" href="nav.xhtml" media-type="application/xhtml+xml" nav/>
    <item id="toc.ncx" href="toc.ncx" media-type="application/x-dtbncx+xml"/>
    <item id="epub.css" href="styles/epub.css" media-type="text/css"/>
    <item id="cover.jpg" href="images/cover.jpg" media-type="image/jpeg" properties="cover-image"/>

    <!-- Content — IN spine -->
    <item id="cover.xhtml" href="cover.xhtml" media-type="application/xhtml+xml"/>
    <item id="title.xhtml" href="title.xhtml" media-type="application/xhtml+xml"/>
    ...
</manifest>
```

## Why This Happens in Auto-Builders

Tools like the `build-epub-python.py` script (in this skill's `scripts/`) use a generic `add()` helper that adds to both manifest and spine. Before May 2026, nav/NCX/CSS were passed through this helper and ended up in the spine. The fix (applied 2026-05-11):

1. Added `in_spine=True` parameter to `add()`
2. Called `add(..., in_spine=False)` for nav, NCX, and CSS

Always verify the output of any auto-generation tool against this reference.
